questionStem: A70-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-month history of progressive swelling that began in his legs and now extends to his lower abdomen. He also has noted fatigue and shortness of breath during this time. He says he lost consciousness briefly while mowing the lawn last week. The patient experienced an episode of chest pain 1 year ago, and coronary angiography at that time disclosed no coronary artery stenosis. He has a 12-year history of severe obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea and has been unable to tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. He also has a 5-year history of hypertension well controlled with hydrochlorothiazide and verapamil. He does not smoke cigarettes. He drinks two 12-0z beers weekly. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses regular rate and rhythm. Jugular venous pressure is 8 cm above the sternal notch/clavicle. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Pulmonary hypertension is one cause of right-sided heart failure in patients with no evidence of left-sided heart failure. Signs suggestive of right-sided heart failure include bilateral lower extremity edema, jugular venous distention, hepatosplenomegaly, and abdominal swelling. There are multiple causes of pulmonary hypertension, including genetic causes, connective tissue disease (eg, lupus), HIV, congenital heart disease, left-sided heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea. Transthoracic echocardiography may be used as an initial screening test for evaluation and may suggest the diagnosis. Further studies include high-resolution CT scan, ventilation-perfusion lung scans, right and left heart catheterization, laboratory studies, and polysomnography. Once the underlying cause of pulmonary hypertension has been identified, treatments aimed at symptomatic relief, including diuretic agents, may be used along with treatment of the underlying cause, such as continuous positive airway pressure in obstructive sleep apnea. For this patient, the most likely cause of pulmonary hypertension is poorly controlled obstructive sleep apnea.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cellulitis (Choice A) presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, and induration. Systemic symptoms, including fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis are often present. The two most common pathogens in cellulitis include Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Choice B) is an obstructive lung disease associated with tobacco use characterized by expiratory airflow obstruction. Chronic symptoms are improved with the use of inhaled long-acting beta agonists, inhaled muscarinic antagonists, and glucocorticoids. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease may cause pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure in patients with a significant smoking history. Deep venous thrombosis (Choice C) may cause lower extremity swelling, pain, and discoloration. Symptoms may be acute in nature, and patients are treated with anticoagulation and/or thrombectomy depending on the severity and location of the thrombus. This patient's clinical presentation is not consistent with a deep venous thrombosis. Left-sided heart failure (Choice D) is a commonly encountered clinical syndrome associated with chronic hypertension and coronary artery disease. Physical examination findings include increased jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema, ascites, hepatojugular reflux, pulmonary crackles, and an S3 or Sq gallop. This presentation supports right-sided heart failure; however, this patient lacks clinical evidence of cardiogenic pulmonary edema, which would suggest left-sided heart failure. Educational Objective: Examination findings suggestive of pulmonary hypertension include those of right-sided heart failure: lower extremity edema, jugular venous distention, hepatosplenomegaly, and abdominal swelling. A common cause of pulmonary hypertension is left-sided heart failure; however, other causes include obstructive sleep apnea and chronic venous thromboembolic disease. correctExplanation: Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures are also called complex partial seizures. As this name suggests, these seizures affect a specific (focal) region of the brain and therefore produce motor or sensory symptoms that are localized to one or a few areas of the body. Patients will be unresponsive during the seizure (impaired awareness). Oral and manual automatisms, as in this patient, are suggestive of a temporal lobe lesion, the most common origin of seizures. Upper limb dystonia and autonomic disturbances such as an epigastric rising sensation can also occur in temporal lobe seizures. Patients may experience visual, auditory, or sensory auras preceding the seizure. Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures are often accompanied by a brief postictal state marked by confusion and fatigue. These seizures will demonstrate localized rhythmic activity with generalized slowing on EEG. The lesion most commonly responsible for temporal lobe epilepsy is mesial temporal sclerosis, also called hippocampal sclerosis. However, a new presentation with progressively worsening frequency and cognitive changes should raise concerns that the cause may be a tumor. MRI of the brain should be ordered to search for a mass lesion. If located, surgical excision of the lesion can be considered.

Other signs of hypoglycemia (tremors, palpitations, diaphoresis) or hyperglycemia (osmotic diuresis, dehydration, altered mental status) are present. Measurement of serum prolactin concentration (Choice B) is part of the workup for pituitary adenomas, which present with headache and bitemporal hemianopsia. Seizures are rare and would not localize to the temporal lobe as in this patient. Urine toxicology screening (Choice C) is useful in the workup of suspected substance use disorder or toxin-related seizures. Causes include stimulants such as cocaine, amphetamines, ecstasy (3,4- methylenedioxymethamphetamine), PCP (phencyclidine), and theophylline and toxins such as strychnine. Seizures tend to be generalized, not focal. A chronic, progressive presentation is more consistent with a structural lesion. Lumbar puncture (Choice E) is useful for the diagnosis of meningitis, encephalitis, or leptomeningeal disease, as well as occult subarachnoid hemorrhage, all of which can cause generalized seizures. Focal seizures in the absence of systemic infectious signs, metastatic cancer, or headache and altered mental status, respectively, are not consistent with any of these causes. The classic triad of symptoms includes episodic vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus. The diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms and audiometric evidence of sensorineural hearing loss. LEMS is an uncommon neurologic condition involving formation of antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels at the neuromuscular junction, commonly as a paraneoplastic phenomenon in association with small cell lung carcinoma. Normally, voltage-gated calcium channels at the axonal terminal bouton open following depolarization, allowing calcium influx, and triggering exocytosis of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles into the synaptic cleft. In LEMS, antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels prevent terminal axonal calcium influx and release of acetylcholine to postsynaptic skeletal muscle cells. Patients classically display a triad of muscular weakness, depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes, and autonomic dysfunction. The muscle weakness and areflexia typically improve with exercise as amounts of acetylcholine accumulate in the synaptic cleft. Autonomic symptoms may include orthostasis, decreased salivation, dry eyes, and erectile dysfunction. Ocular and bulbar symptoms may occur later in the disease following onset of proximal muscle weakness and may include dysphagia, diplopia, and ptosis. The diagnosis is confirmed with nerve conduction studies and electromyography with exercise testing.

Patients typically have a positive family history. Common symptoms include muscular weakness, fatigue, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens toward the end of the day, along with dysphagia and potential respiratory distress. It is closely related to dermatomyositis; however, unlike dermatomyositis, it does not present with cutaneous findings. questionStem: An otherwise healthy 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of worsening left-sided headache. The pain, which is worse when she is physically active and when she lies down, is partially relieved by 325-mg aspirin. One month ago, she was involved in a motor vehicle collision in which she was the restrained driver. Her car was hit broadside from the left, and she says that she hit her head on the window. She had brief loss of consciousness, and a bump later developed on the left side of her head. She refused medical attention from paramedics. Her pulse is 60/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg. Deep tendon reflexes are mildly increased on the right compared with the left. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An injury of which of the following structures is the most likely cause of her signs and symptoms?
correctExplanation: Shearing of the bridging veins in the subdural space is the cause of subdural hematoma (SDH). Head trauma, the use of anticoagulants, physical abuse, alcohol use disorder, cerebral atrophy, and malignancy are associated with an increased risk for SDH. On imaging, SDH appears as a crescent-shaped collection abutting the internal surface of the skull, not bound by suture lines. In some cases, the SDH may be large enough to compress adjacent brain parenchyma, displacing the cerebral hemisphere. Thus, presentation can include subacute-onset headache, focal neurologic deficits, altered mental status, seizures, herniation syndromes, and signs of increased intracranial pressure such as vomiting and papilledema. Patients may manifest upper motor neuron examination findings such as spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar reflex (Babinski sign). Elderly patients are at risk for cerebral atrophy, which places traction on bridging cortical veins. In this setting, minor trauma such as falls can result in shearing of the veins leading to hemorrhage. Untreated, the SDH may continue to grow. The intracranial compartment is a fixed space within a rigid skull; pathologic lesions such as SDH can result in midline shift and herniation of central nervous system structures if large enough. When such mass effect is present or at risk for developing, surgical interventions such as decompressive burr holes or a craniotomy may be indicated to evacuate the hematoma.

Occlusion of the middle cerebral artery leads to contralateral hemiparesis and contralateral sensory deficit of the face and upper extremities. Occlusion of the middle cerebral artery supplying the dominant hemisphere (usually the left hemisphere) leads to aphasia, while occlusion of the middle cerebral artery supplying the nondominant hemisphere results in hemineglect. questionStem: A77-year-old man is brought to the emergency department immediately after a 30-minute episode of spinning vertigo and right facial and upper extremity numbness that occurred while he was shopping at a grocery store. He had a similar episode of spinning vertigo and slurred speech 1 month ago that lasted for 1 hour. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and coronary artery disease. Medications include atenolol, chlorthalidone, glyburide, and aspirin. His pulse is 86/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. There is horizontal left-beating nystagmus that worsens with left gaze. Sensation is absent to pinprick over the right side of the face. Hearing is reduced bilaterally to finger rub. Cardiac examination shows bilateral supraclavicular and carotid bruits. A grade 2/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard at the cardiac base. Muscle strength is normal throughout. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. Romberg sign is positive, and he has a broad-based gait. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency is often caused by atherosclerosis leading to decreased posterior circulation, most commonly at or near the vertebrobasilar artery junction. Symptoms of vertebrobasilar insufficiency can include vertigo, light-headedness, dysequilibrium, ataxia, and nystagmus (due to transiently decreased blood supply to the vestibular nuclei). Patients can have difficulty walking or lean while standing upright without support (Romberg sign). Upper motor neuron signs such as hyperreflexia and Babinski sign point to a central cause of this patient's vertigo. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency can be transient, such as with a transient ischemic attack, or cause infarction of the lateral medulla. Patients can also present with loss of pain and temperature sensation of the ipsilateral face and contralateral extremities.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acoustic neuroma (Choice A) presents with symptoms of hearing loss, vertigo, and ataxia, often slow in onset and progressive over a subacute to chronic period. Acoustic neuromas may exert mass effect on cranial nerves within their proximity or invade the nerves from which they arise, often the facial nerve, vestibulocochlear nerve, or adjacent nerves, resulting in facial asymmetry and/or diminished hearing or tinnitus. Bilateral hyperreflexia and Babinski sign are more suggestive of vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Benign positional vertigo (Choice B) is a common cause of vertigo that occurs due to a calcium carbonate particle (otoconium) that gets displaced from the otolith organs into the adjacent semicircular canals, leading to the erroneous sensation of position change. Patients typically present with episodic vertigo with nystagmus, nausea, and normal hearing. Since it is a peripheral cause of vertigo, patients would not have upper motor neuron signs suggestive of a central cause of vertigo. Carotid stenosis (Choice C) can cause decreased flow to the brain or embolic events causing cerebrovascular ischemia. Patients can have a carotid bruit on examination. Thalamic infarction (Choice D) such as with an ischemic stroke can cause specific neurologic deficits depending on which thalamic nuclei are involved, including visual deficits, hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, and/or language deficits. It is not typically associated with vertigo. Vestibulitis (Choice F) is an idiopathic localized vulvar pain syndrome, also known as vulvodynia. It is not associated with neurologic deficits. Vestibular neuritis is an inflammation of the vestibulocochlear nerve, resulting in peripheral vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and gait instability. It is usually preceded by a viral illness and does not typically cause hearing loss. Educational Objective: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency is often caused by atherosclerosis and decreased perfusion of the posterior circulation, leading to vertigo, light-headedness, dysequilibrium, ataxia, and nystagmus.
